b: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur sees the Russian auteur tracing the sociopolitical landscape of his home country for the first time since a highly publicized, years-long battle with COVID complications and his subsequent flight to France. Shot in Latvia but set in Russia, Minotaur shows that Zvyagintsev’s cinema has lost none of its quietly devastating intellectual rigor despite his new status as an outsider looking in from afar.

Minotaur takes place in 2022 and concerns well-heeled business executive Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), his glamorous wife, Galina (Iris Lebedeva), and their teenage son, Seryozha (Boris Kudrin), who inhabit a handsome though nondescript dacha in the Russian provinces. Though they’re ostensibly a happy family who want for nothing, there are signs of a gulf between Gleb and Galina, whose interactions are cordial yet cold.

At the office, Gleb is tasked by the local government with selecting fourteen of his employees for conscription to support Russia’s invasion of neighboring Ukraine. This, combined with Galina’s seemingly innocent morning jaunts to the local café and hushed phone calls, starts to eat away at Gleb, who hires a detective to find out whether his wife is being faithful to him as the clock runs out on deciding who he must send to an almost certain death.

A loose adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 infidelity drama The Unfaithful Wife, Minotaur becomes an indictment of class, complicity, and an entire nation, its intellectual and thematic fingers reaching far beyond the couple at its center. I sat down with the writer-director to discuss Minotaur as an extension of his previous work, myth as a frame through which to view his art, and the film’s stunning (yet withholding) final image.

In Minotaur, as in all of your films, the personal and the political are totally inextricable. Though the film is very obviously grappling with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, would you say there’s an element here of you processing your new reality after your illness and relocation to France?

I wouldn’t say my personal story is somehow connected to the film. Of course, these have been a few very dramatic pages from my biography: leaving my house, leaving my country, my culture, my language, and moving to a completely different reality at 58 years old. Adjusting to new circumstances, a new reality, was difficult, but I wouldn’t necessarily connect those things.

I’m at the point where all I have is my reputation in the eyes of the people who make decisions about films now in Europe and America. In a lot of ways, I had to restart my career and my life in general when I moved to France: new circumstances, new rules, new conditions, new everything. We knew, of course, that making a film after 2022, we could not ignore what is going on in the larger context. The catastrophe, the historical tragedy that’s going on with Russia and Ukraine, would have to be intertwined with a smaller, more intimate human story.
This being your first film made outside of Russia, do you see Minotaur as marking a shift in your artistic perspective? Or do you view it more as an extension of what came before?

I think that there’s a continuity between this film and all the previous films. Maybe people viewing it from the outside would have a different perspective on that, and they can judge or have their own opinions about the style, the rhythm, and other visual aspects, but I think that the approach is the same. It’s just one continuous story across all the films.

You had wanted to adapt The Unfaithful Wife for quite a while, but it really feels like this film couldn’t exist or resonate as it does without the war. What, for you, makes an infidelity drama the right metaphor for this specific conflict?

I think the two things intertwine quite easily. In Chabrol’s film, if you’ve seen the original, there is a space—his office life, his social life—that’s done in a very formal way. I thought it was a gap that I wanted to fill in if I was going to make an adaptation. And, of course, in 2022, the events that were going on in Russia and Ukraine filled in the social and political aspect of the film.
The title of the film echoes that of one of your earlier films, 2014’s Leviathan, so I’m curious: Why are you drawn to mythological beasts as a frame through which to view your sociopolitical themes?

Speaking of Leviathan, that title came to us naturally because it’s from the Book of Job, in which he loses one thing after another until he’s left with nothing: his house, his cattle, his family. It’s an Old Testament story. And then, finally, he meets with God, who tells him about Leviathan. At the same time, I was meeting with a friend of mine back then, and she told me about Hobbes and his book, which I didn’t know anything about. It’s from 1651, and it’s called Leviathan or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Commonwealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil.

As for Minotaur, I had a friend in Russia, an entrepreneur, who called me in ’22 and told me that he had been summoned to the mayor’s office, where he was told that there were quotas for every entrepreneur to send a certain number of employees to the front line. I thought it was an incredible insight and that people would be surprised when they saw that in the film. Of course, everything they try to keep secret becomes known eventually, and so, about a month before the film premiered at Cannes, there was an article in the independent press that cited a few such cases, kind of like what we show in the film. So it was something that was happening all around the country. And the fourteen people, as in the Greek myth, are a comment on human sacrifice.

So the title Minotaur has two sides to it. The first is social and political. [And] on a personal, intimate side, there’s a book called The Physiology of Marriage by Honoré de Balzac, which he wrote when he was a very young man, and he talks about family life as a labyrinth in which the husband wanders around, watching his wife anxiously, worrying that there might be someone else in this relationship, and observing her behavior to see if she has secrets that she’s hiding. In a certain moment, as Balzac writes, there might be a lover who jumps out from around the corner and “Minotaurizes”—so he makes it into a verb—the husband.
I’m very taken with the film’s final image, which is presented as footage captured by Gleb and Galina’s son, Seryozha, on his iPhone. Did you shoot it, or was it sourced elsewhere?

In 2023, a very good friend of mine, Vladimir Mashkov, who is an actor and a photographer, a very talented guy, showed it to me. He takes a lot of photos and videos, even in his daily life. He sent me that video. The original lasted for five minutes, but I could not avert my eyes. It was so beautiful. So I told Vladimir that he should not give it away, that I absolutely would take this video from him and just think about where we could include it. My only fear was how it would look on the big screen because, of course, it was shot on an iPhone in 4K, and it was something that he made for himself. But when we finally saw it on the big screen and I realized that it looks as good as it does on the smaller screen, I was just very relieved and very happy. I want to be an Apple ambassador after all I’ve been through! [laughs]
And within the context of the film, where did the decision come from to mediate the final image through the son’s phone camera?

That shot kind of puts an end to the boy’s story. It sums up his story, because in the beginning, he is trying to do some drawings, and he shoots this island across the river that we call the Island of the Dead. He obviously has an artistic gift, and so this final image is him observing reality, his look at reality. That’s why we wanted to end with that.
